title: Contemplation to attain love
hook: love shows itself in deeds; take, Lord, receive

segments.voice: Yesterday, the fourth week: the risen Christ as consoler, with a name, a walk, a breakfast on the beach. Your line was the consoler.

After the fourth week, the Exercises turn to a contemplation, and Ignatius opens it with two short remarks before any prayer at all. First: love ought to show itself more in deeds than in words. Second: love is a sharing. The lover gives the beloved what they have, and the beloved gives back. Two sentences, plain as a kitchen table. No grand theory of love. Everything that follows hangs from them, including a short prayer of offering, written right into the text.
screen: `MORE IN DEEDS THAN IN WORDS.` → `LOVE IS A SHARING.` → `THEN, A PRAYER.`

segments.voice: The contemplation to attain love asks the person to look back over everything received. Creation. Redemption. The particular gifts of one's own life: the people, the chances, the mercies. Ignatius says to ponder how much God has done, and how God wants to give, as far as possible, God's own self. Then the two remarks come back. If love is a sharing, and God has given this much, what does a person give back? Ignatius answers with a prayer, offered as if by someone moved by great love. It's known by its first Latin word, Suscipe: receive. In substance it goes like this. Take, Lord, receive all my liberty, my memory, my understanding, my whole will, everything I have and possess. You gave it to me; I give it back. It's all yours; dispose of it as you will. Give me only your love and your grace; that is enough for me. Look at what is offered: not money, not a list of good works, but freedom, memory, mind and will, the very things the Exercises have been training all along. Indifference, discernment, the choice made from the end. All of it, handed back. And what is asked in return: only love and grace. The First Letter of John, in the Douay-Rheims, makes the same point about deeds: "let us not love in word, nor in tongue, but in deed, and in truth." So the Suscipe is not meant to stay a sentence.
screen: `LOOK BACK AT WHAT YOU'VE BEEN GIVEN.` · `IF LOVE IS SHARING, WHAT GOES BACK?` · `LIBERTY, MEMORY, UNDERSTANDING, WILL.` · `ONLY LOVE AND GRACE.` · then, large: `IN DEED, AND IN TRUTH.`

segments.voice: Let your hands rest open. If you know the Suscipe, pray it slowly, a phrase on each breath; if not, use today's line, take, Lord, receive, and name one at a time what Ignatius offers: my freedom, my memory, my mind, my will. If you don't pray, sit with the question underneath it: what am I holding that I could hand over?
Suscipe. Receive: the first word of Ignatius's prayer of offering, which hands back freedom, memory, mind and will, and asks only for love and grace. Today's word.
Your line: take, Lord, receive. Love shows itself more in deeds than in words. That's day one thousand two hundred sixty-one.

howItsDone: The Suscipe closes the Spiritual Exercises' contemplation to attain love; some who pray in the Ignatian way say it at the end of a retreat, and some pray it daily.

chat.says: What do you actually give God in Ignatius's Suscipe prayer?
options: Your freedom, memory, understanding and will, all you have; you ask only for love and grace.
A promise of regular money and good works each week, offered in exchange for God's help.
Only your daily plans, since Ignatius says your memory and mind should stay your own.

notes: The Suscipe is given only 'in substance' (paraphrased), not quoted, because no translation of the Exercises is on the public-domain list. The practice invites those who know it to pray it; no new prayer is written. Confirm the paraphrase.

The two preliminary remarks (no. 230–231) and the first point (no. 234: benefits received, God desiring to give himself) are paraphrased. Points two to four (God dwelling and working in all things) are left for tomorrow, 'God in all things'.
Latin 'Suscipe' as the first word of the Latin version ('Suscipe, Domine, universam meam libertatem'); confirm, and confirm the ecclesiastical pronunciation SOO-shee-peh.
